title: Abd al-Rahman III
hookLine: who declared a caliphate in Cordoba

lines: A NOTE FOUND AFTER HIS DEATH.
ONLY A HANDFUL OF HAPPY DAYS.
cards: A story is told in the later histories of al-Andalus. When a great ruler of Cordoba died, after a long reign of victories, building and wealth, a note was found among his things in his own hand.
On it he had counted the days of his life when he had been truly happy, free of worry. There were only a handful. Nobody can say for certain it happened that way.
But it's told about this man for a reason: he had everything a ruler could want, and the story says it wasn't enough. His name was Abd al-Rahman III.

teach.b: He came to power young, over a land in pieces. Rebels held hill fortresses; cities obeyed when it suited them. He spent years bringing them back under Cordoba's rule.
Then he did something bold. Rulers of al-Andalus before him had called themselves emir, prince. He took the title caliph, and commander of the faithful.
Why? In Baghdad, the Abbasid caliph had grown weak. In North Africa, the Fatimids had declared a caliphate of their own, led by Isma'ili Shia imams.
Abd al-Rahman answered by claiming the title for Cordoba: three caliphs at once, east, North Africa and far west.

For Sunni Muslims, a caliph is the successor who leads the community; Shia Muslims hold that rightful leadership belongs to the Imams of the Prophet's family. The title meant different things depending on who was asking.
He built a palace city outside it, Madinat al-Zahra, with halls of marble and gardens. Envoys came from distant kings. A Jewish physician, Hasdai ibn Shaprut, served at his court.

teach.h: A GOLDEN AGE HAS A BILL.
teach.b: But a golden age has a bill: armies, taxes, campaigns against neighbors, enslaved servants and soldiers in the palace.
Later, under his descendants, the caliphate broke apart in civil war, and the palace city was looted and left in ruins.
The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "Everyone that is thereon will pass away; There remaineth but the Countenance of thy Lord of Might and Glory."

how: The caliphate of Cordoba is remembered in Muslim histories as part of al-Andalus's story of learning and building, and visitors today can walk the excavated ruins of Madinat al-Zahra near Cordoba.

a judge who rules on questions of family law

his palace city, later left in ruins

games.q: you rule Cordoba as emir. in North Africa, the Fatimids have declared a caliphate, and the caliph in Baghdad is weak. what do you do?
o: stay an emir and keep your head down.
declare yourself caliph, commander of the faithful.
games.why: Abd al-Rahman III took the title caliph for Cordoba, so for a time there were caliphs in the east, in North Africa and in the west.

practice: Bring to mind a time people call golden, in history, in a family, maybe in your own life, and remember what was really good about it.

Then ask, gently: whose work, whose quiet suffering held it up, and who doesn't appear in the story? Hold the light and the bill side by side, and if you pray, remember the ones who paid, and if not, just keep them in view.

wordCard.voice: Caliph. The title Abd al-Rahman III took for Cordoba, after ruling as emir, building Madinat al-Zahra and, the story says, counting only a handful of happy days. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: caliph, a successor or deputy; the title Abd al-Rahman III took.

carryVoice: Your line: a western caliphate. Three caliphs at once, and a palace city left in ruins. Day nine hundred thirty-six, done.
